messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Re: Using dsm without coordinates?
messages.body_plain:
Katy

If your interest is in estimating fish density using distance sampling, you need not use density surface modelling.  Conventional distance sampling quite happily can produce density estimates taking into account sources of variation in detectability caused by various factors you mentioned.

Density surface modelling attempts to estimate differences in animal density related to environmental covariates.  The covariates are spatially referenced, as are the animal locations.  Density surface models model the relationship between counts (adjusted for incomplete detectability) and the covariates using the locations (coordinates) of both to establish the correspondence of the two types of data.  Without animal locations the modelling process cannot succeed.  It is very much the case that knowing the manner in which data are to be analysed needs to be considered prior to the collection data.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] RE: Spatial autocorrelation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gemma, hi listfolk,

I think this question is hard to answer in general and depends at least
a little on the model that you fitted and your inferential goal.

There probably is spatial autocorrelation along your transects, but you
may be already modelling that via either a smooth of space or other
terms in your model that vary at the same scale (e.g. what appears to be
autocorrelation may be down to prey patches, which you might be able to
model via some covariate, like primary productivity or just a smooth of
space). In some sense we are interested in the autocorrelation
conditional on the model that has been fitted -- the residual
autocorrelation. Models with smooths of space in them may be already
taking this into account, provided they can be flexible enough.

So, you may not need to worry about this. Using a correllogram or
plotting box plots of the residuals by spatial area may be an easy way
to address this (see, e.g. Marra, Miller and Zanin (2011)).

Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave

Marra, G., Miller, D. L., & Zanin, L. (2011). Modelling the
spatiotemporal distribution of the incidence of resident foreign
population. Statistica Neerlandica, 66(2), 133–160.
http://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9574.2011.00500.x

messages.body_plain:
Giles

Taking your questions in random order:  warnings do not necessarily mean there are problems with the analysis--warnings indicate have a look at the output to see if there is anything amiss.

I suspect there is an error in one of the last two lines of your table.  If two models have the same AIC and the same confidence intervals, they should have the same estimate of abundance (982 vs 932).

For your central question regarding how to select the most appropriate model:  AIC will rank amongst competing models; we call AIC a "relative" measure of fit.  AIC measures the performance of models relative to one another, another step is needed to determine whether models with low AIC values actually fit the observed data.  In addition to using AIC and goodness of fit measures, you will also use your understanding of the habitat and the species you are studying.  These statistics serve as guides--if the rules regarding model selection were absolute, we would program the rules into Distance and have the programme produce the 'correct' answer.  There remains some 'art' to the model selection process.

You would also want to include an absolute measure of fit--namely a goodness of fit test.  If you have analysed exact distances, Distance will produce Kolomogorov-Smirnov (K-S) and Cramer-von Mises (CvM) tests of fit.  You should use models that fit the detection data.  For point transect data, Distance produces two different plots, the g(x) plots (you have shown) and the "pdf" plots.  It is the pdf plots that give a better indication of the fit of the models to your data (along with the K-S/CvM test results).

Finally, confidence interval size should *not* be used to select a model.  Choosing a model with a small confidence interval heightens the chance that the true abundance of the population does not fall within that small confidence interval.

The challenge with the data you show is the large number of detections in the first histogram interval (I cannot read the width of that bin).  Given these birds are often on the ground under cover, I would have thought they would be hard to detect at close distances.  You might want to re-examine the data with smaller bin widths and perhaps truncate more of your data where there are few detections at large distances.  You are getting a discrepancy in abundance estimates because some models are trying to fit that spike at small distances (hazard rate models) and other models (uniform with adjustments) are not trying to fit the spike.  The central question in your analysis is whether that spike is real or an artefact of the manner in which the histograms are created.  Only those who collected the data can answer that question.

Hugo

Smearing to deal with rounding is not supported in the ds() function in the Distance R package.

As an alternative, you can specify the cut points of bins into which to place your perpendicular distance data prior to analysis.  The key cut point selection is to place them in such a way as your heaped distances fall near the centre of the bins.  The intention is to specify bins such that they accurately represent where the detected animal may have been (but was inaccurately recorded by the observers).

I hope that answers your question.

The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM) is hosting two linked workshops in the summer of 2016 at the University of St. Andrews, Scotland.
The first workshop (16-19 August) will run at an introductory level, and will focus on distance sampling methods, largely described in the standard reference book "Introduction to Distance Sampling." The workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and participants will learn how to use the program "Distance." Participants will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and methods of analysis for distance sampling surveys.

The advanced distance sampling workshop (22-25 August) will include advanced treatment of analyses in which detectability on the transect line is not assumed to be perfect (the so-called g(0) problem) and spatial (or density surface) modelling. We will showcase a series of R packages for performing standard as well as sophisticated analyses in R.

For all workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data sets, and can expect to perform preliminary analyses of their data.  Participants can use our computers or bring their own laptops.

Adiran

I didn't phrase my answer quite correctly.  It is the number of adjustment terms that can be fitted that is being adjusted, rather than the number of bins.  I replied to quickly at the end of the day.

The message is that the number of points of support for your models is the number of bins of your distances.  The messages Distance is producing reflects the tension between number of parameters and number of data points (points of support).  Take the hazard rate key function; it has 2 parameters.  Distance is noting that the hazard can only support a maximum of 2 additional parameters associated with adjustment terms, bringing total number of estimated parameters to a maximum of 4.  There is one degree of freedom (5 data - 4 parameters) remaining to assess goodness of fit.

Trying to fit a 4 parameter model with only 5 data points will be a challenge--repeating the process 999 times will, as you experienced, eventually lead to "convergence failure".  You also note your received a warning that parameter estimates are highly correlated--that arises from over-parametrised models (over-parametrised in the sense that you have nearly as many parameters as data points).

Given the tension between parameter count and data points (bins), it is sensible to either restrain the number of parameters estimated or increase the number of bins.  However, I presume you set the number of bins to 5 for some other reason.

messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

The various online sources (paper appendices, St Andrews resources, etc. – thanks to all!) have greatly assisted me to generate a dsm map and estimates of abundance. However, I am making a conversion error somewhere in this process (alternatively, I have found the most abundant animal known to man).

I will be extremely happy if someone with a keen eye can look through the following and explain to me where I am going wrong with the abundance prediction.

I have the following data contained in the dataframe ‘distdata’ and use it to fit a detection function. Distance was recorded in meter (binned analysis), and transect length (Effort) in kilometre (median transect length = 65 km)

hr.obs  <-  ds(distdata, key="hr", adjustment=NULL,  truncation=list(left=35.2,right=345.73),

                convert.units = 0.001, formula=~as.factor(Observer))

[From ?ds: “Effort was entered in kilometers and Area in square kilometers and distance in meters then using convert.units=0.001 would convert meters to kilometers, density would be expressed in square kilometres”].

All good until here, I believe. Now I would like to fit a dsm:

For this, I use

dsm.count <- dsm(count~s(x,y, k = 20),

             ddf.obj= hr.obs,

                         segment.data = segdata,

                         observation.data=obsdata,

                         convert.units = 1/1000,

                         family=nb(), method="REML")

segdata also contains an effort column, but here ‘Effort’ refers to segment length (in km), and not transect length (median segment length = 6 km) (n = 281 segments)

I use convert.units = 1/1000 here.

I quote from ?dsm: “For example: if distances are in metres and segment lengths are in kilometres setting convert.units=1000 will lead to the analysis being in metres. Setting convert.units=1/1000 will lead to the analysis being in kilometres. The conversion factor will be applied to 'segment.area' if that is specified. [Note that I did not specify segment.area, so this is taken as multiplying the 'Effort' column in the 'segment.data' by the (right minus left) truncation distance for the 'ddf.obj'].

Finally, I do the prediction to an x/y grid of 25 km by 25 km (preddata)

off.set = 625 * 1000 * 1000

pp <- predict(dsm.count, preddata, off.set)

sum(pp, na.rm=TRUE)

[1] Overabundance

I noticed that using convert.units = 1000 in the dsm step would give me believable abundance estimates. But this estimates density in meter squared, not km2?

Assuming I have given enough information here for someone to spot the mistake (I kind of hope there is one in the conversions I used), I would like to ask a related question.

Would the analysis differ in any way if I used Nhat instead of count as the response variable of the dsm?

With thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris, hi listfolk,

Glad to hear that you're finding the online resources useful!

Relatively minor point: the convert.units argument is only necessary for
ds() when you're estimating abundance at the same time. If you're just
fitting a detection function you don't need to set it.

In dsm() convert.units is used to correctly calculate the segment area
by ensuring that the segment width (which would be the strip width for
the detection function) is in the same units as the segment length (the
Effort column).

A quick check that you're doing the right thing is that:

(345.73-35.2)*2 = strip width in metres

So the segment.area column in the dsm.count$data data.frame should equal
the Effort column multiplied by the above, in the correct units -- so
multiplying the above by 1/1000 to get the area in km. This sounds right
from what you've said.

The predictions are I think where things go wrong... The offset is the
area of the cells in the same units as the segment areas. So the offset
should be in km. Your line:

 > off.set = 625 * 1000 * 1000

is calculating the offset in m^2 not km^2, so your estimated should be
1000^2 times too big (that's big!).

Just setting off.set to be 625 should solve this problem.

To your additional question on Nhat vs. count -- using "Nhat" as the
response will calculate the Horvitz-Thompson estimate per segment and
use that as the response in the dsm. There will be differences in the
analysis, as you're using a different response, though these should not
be too big. There are sometimes good reasons to do this (for example
when detection-level covariates vary at scales smaller than the
segment), but if you can get away with using count I think (personal
opinion) it makes more sense to stick to counts as response, as it's
closer to what you actually saw and then your use of count distributions
as the response is more coherent.

Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] 'flatfile' vs 'tables'
messages.body_plain:
Olivier

Thanks for using the Distance package and contributing to this list.

The Distance package in general and the ds() function in particular, were developed to make it easier to use the functions living inside the package mrds.  The functions inside mrds use the data structure of tables (region.table, sample.table and obs.table) for performing distance sampling analysis.  The ds() function can work either with data in the 'tables' format, or it can use data provided in the 'flatfile' format from which it re-organised data into the 'tables' format.

We have found most users have their data in the 'flatfile' format, whereas they need to do some wrestling with their data to conform to the 'tables' format.  Hence ds() was extended to provide the ability to do that wrestling.

Specifically about the 'object' field.  That does indeed contain simply a sequential numbering of the observations (clusters if your detections were of clusters).  The 'object' field is another example of "retro-fitting" of data into a format expected by the functions in mrds.

Hope that is helpful.

messages.body_plain:
Hello Distance listserv,

I am writing to the list for the first time to kindly ask for help with designing a survey. More specifically I am having problems with preparing a coverage layer in Distance that adopts a matching projected coordinate system to that of the parent and child layers.  In my study I have chosen to use line transects to sample a target butterfly population across a relatively modest area (approximately 2.5 km2) comprised of multiple fields of state managed grasslands here in the eastern USA.  I’m using Distance 6.2 Release 1 on Windows 7 via the Parallels 10 for Mac application.

I have imported shapefiles for the global and strata layers by copying them into the project folder and I am able to prepare maps of these in Distance and ensure that everything looks correct.  By checking the “Data Layer Properties” window in Distance I can see that the Geographic Coordinate System for the global layer is: NAD 1983 NSRS2007 UTM Zone 18N and this differs only slightly for the Strata layer: NAD 1983 UTM Zone 18N.  The projection for both layers is the Transverse Mercator and the units have been set to “meters”.  When adding these two layers to a map in Distance I find that they overlap perfectly, just as intended.

When I attempt to add a coverage layer, there seems to be a problem with getting the geographic coordinate system for all layers to match.  After creating the coverage layer and attempting to map it, I find that the specified grid does not fall overtop the global and strata layers and the points end up distributed wildly in space.  When I “zoom to extent” with all 3 layers selected only a single point comes into view and the global and strata layers are then no longer visible.  After checking the layer properties for the coverage layer in Distance again it seems that the geographic coordinate system and projection are largely the same (i.e. North American 1983 with all the appropriate corresponding Projection Parameters) but only the Zone, 18N hasn’t been specified.  Furthermore there is no projected coordinate system specified in the first line of the coordinate system information that appears when clicking on the "Geographic data" tab of the Data Layer Properties dialogue. I have double-checked and ensured that the shapefile units for all layers have been set to meters.

Although my GIS knowledge is far from extensive, I have tried a few potential fixes to this already. Firstly I have been able to prepare otherwise meaningful designs for the study by ensuring that the Geographic Coordinate System and Projection are set to “None” for all layers including by also setting the coordinate system to “none” by using the “Project Properties” menu.  I am able to experiment with different designs and calculate coverage probability statistics for each one without any problems.  In fact based on the results of these explorations I feel that I have identified an otherwise suitable design for the study yet when I attempt to map the sampler starting and end points in ArcMap I am unable to do so.  So my first question is, “Is there is a way to work backward and convert these simple linear coordinates to the appropriate coordinate system using the results of the survey design engine when geographic coordinate system has been set to “none”?  I sense that the answer to this question is probably “no” although if it provides a solution, of course that is all that I’m after.  That being said, if as a solution this approach is more complex than getting the coordinate system of the coverage layer to correspond correctly to the geo-referenced global and child layers I’d rather keep things as simple as possible and run the designs again in Distance with a geocoordinate system that translates correctly across all layers.

Setting the North American 1983 coordinate system to Zone 18N is unavailable in Distance so I also tried to change the coordinate system for the global and child layers after import so that they match that of the coverage layer.  After doing the and attempting to create the coverage layer the warning message, “No points fell within the survey area” appears.  Although this doesn’t seem possible I have changed the spacing between grid points to as low as a few meters, just for the sake of argument, but the software returns the same warning message.

I have also tried to copy and rename the projection file (i.e. .prj file) that is associated with the Global layer and rename it in the Project folder using the same name as the coverage layer.  The coverage layer that is created does not overlay the global and strata layers and the grid points are spread wildly in space as before.

I have done my best to research the archives on the issue and although there are some relevant posts where users encountered the same problem where none of their grid points fell within their survey areas, none of these have solved my problem.  I’m aware that in the Distance user’s manual the authors advise that in some cases geometry problems are responsible for the design engine responding strangely, however I have been unable to link to the appropriate page on the ESRI website where these issues are addressed at greater length.  Furthermore, I suspect this is not the problem I’m having since my global and strata layers map correctly by themselves.

In any case, if anyone can please advise me on this problem and coming up with a solution, I would really appreciate it.  We're so eager to adopt a design for this study and start implementing it in the field!

Thanks,

Matthew

There is no simple formula to answer the sample size question you ask.  Recognize you are on the low end of fitting a detection function in conventional terms with the numbers of detections you note (if they were to have come from a single observer).
